> AGENT

This is a clean, battle-tested load_inline variant. The key difference from our v2: it uses the "lifted scale" pattern (accumulate unscaled dot products per block, then multiply by scales once) but is still a naive 1-thread-per-element approach. Our v2 should be faster due to shared memory tiling.

However, this autoresearch version has a critical difference — it uses the **shuffled** B weights and scales (B_shuffle, B_scale_sh) instead of re-quantizing B from scratch. This is important: B is pre-quantized and pre-shuffled by `generate_input()`. Let me check if our v2 kernel is correctly using the pre-processed B data.

Looking at our v2 `custom_kernel`, we re-quantize B from scratch:
```python
B_q_raw, B_scale_e8m0 = dynamic_mxfp4_quant(B.contiguous())
```

This is wasteful — B is already quantized in the input tuple. The autoresearch version uses `B_shuffle.view(torch.uint8)` and `B_scale_sh.view(torch.uint8)` directly. However, their kernel receives shuffled data, while our v2 kernel expects un-shuffled layout.

The fundamental issue: **shuffled** data is optimized for aiter's internal tile coalescing pattern, not for our custom kernel's sequential byte access. Our v2 should use **un-shuffled** B data. Let me fix this:

Here are the search results for your query about AMD MI355X gfx950 MFMA MXFP4 kernel optimization. While no results specifically mention `load_inline`, there is a wealth of relevant information across several sources:

---

### 1. Hardware-Specific Optimizations & MFMA (ROCm Composable Kernel)
The gfx950 architecture introduces MicroScaling (MX) formats with hardware-accelerated scale MFMA instructions. The increased LDS capacity on gfx950 enables larger tile sizes and more aggressive blocking strategies, improving performance for memory-intensive operations. The `mfma_scale_*` instructions integrate dequantization with matrix multiplication: each instruction takes separate scale factors for A and B matrices.

**Source:** [DeepWiki - ROCm Composable Kernel](https://deepwiki.com/ROCm/composable_kernel/6.2-hardware-specific-optimizations-and-mfma)

---

### 2. High-Accuracy MXFP4 on AMD GPUs (ROCm Blog)
AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs natively support both FP4 and FP6 datatypes, enabling exceptional AI acceleration. Quark-quantized models can be deployed on AMD Instinct™ MI355 GPUs, which provide native support for FP4, FP6, and mixed-precision FP4-FP6 through Matrix Fused Multiply Add (MFMA) scale instructions. Results show that MXFP4 achieves nearly lossless accuracy on super-large models when combined with advanced PTQ algorithms.

**Source:** [ROCm Blog - MXFP4/MXFP6 Quantization](https://rocm.blogs.amd.com/software-tools-optimization/mxfp4-mxfp6-quantization/README.html)

---

### 3. FP8 GEMM Optimization on CDNA4 (MI355X) — March 2026
This post shows how to use Matrix Cores in GEMM kernels, with a particular focus on optimizing an FP8 GEMM kernel on the AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs. The CDNA™4 architecture increases LDS capacity and read bandwidth (160 KB, 256 B/clk), expands the per-lane GLOBAL_LOAD_LDS transfer width (128-bit vs. 32-bit), and adds broader low-precision matrix-core support, including FP4/FP6 dense MFMA and block-scaled MFMA instructions. By applying techniques such as double buffering, Matrix Core instructions, LDS swizzled memory access, fine-grained instruction scheduling, and the 8-wave ping-pong algorithm design, they achieved performance comparable to hipBLASLt. Importantly, this was accomplished without writing the kernel in assembly; instead, they remained at the HIP/C++ level throughout the process.

**Source:** [ROCm Blog - FP8 GEMM Optimization on CDNA4](https://rocm.blogs.amd.com/software-tools-optimization/cdna4-gemm-kernels/README.html)

---

### 4. GPU MODE Hackathon — MXFP4 Kernel Challenges on MI355X
Phase 1 consists of three kernel optimization problems, all based on operations critical to DeepSeek-R1 model inference on AMD MI355X GPUs. These include optimizing MLA (Multi-Latent Attention) decode and implementing a fused MoE (Mixture of Experts) layer with MXFP4 weight quantization, optimized for DeepSeek-R1's expert architecture. The hackathon uses the `aiter` library with functions like `dynamic_mxfp4_quant` and `mxfp4_to_f32`.

**Source:** [GitHub - AMD GPU MODE Hackathon Phase 1](https://github.com/oldzhu/amd202602/blob/main/AMD_GPU_MODE_Hackathon_Phase1_Preparation.md)

---

### 5. MFMA High Precision Mode for GFX950
Linux 6.15 allows setting a new "HIGH_PRECISION" mode for the Matrix Fused Multiply Add (MFMA) instructions on the AMD matrix cores. This MFMA high precision mode is only implemented with GFX950 and has no impact for other GPUs.

**Source:** [Phoronix - AMD High Precision MI350X](https://www.phoronix.com/news/AMD-HSA-High-Precision-MI350X)

---

### 6. MLPerf Inference v6.0 — MXFP4 on MI355X (April 2026)
The MLPerf Inference v6.0 benchmark results were released on April 1st 2026, with AMD showcasing the performance of the MI355X system. The weights and activations of all applicable PyTorch modules were quantized to OCP MXFP4 or OCP FP8-e4m3 formats. The MI355X-ROCm integration features robust 4-bit floating-point (FP4) precision support that delivers up to 20 petaflops of performance with 288 GB of HBM3 memory and 8TB/s memory bandwidth.

**Source:** [ROCm Blog - MLPerf Inference v6.0](https://rocm.blogs.amd.com/artificial-intelligence/mlperf-inference-v6.0/README.html)

---

### 7. IREE — MXFP4 K Tile Size Optimization for gfx950
For the shape (M, N, K) = (8192, 8192, 8192), the existing K tile size config resulted in 32 MFMAs per workgroup, which might explain the lack of software pipelining due to too many elements being processed per loop iteration. A PR offering one possible solution yielded a 5x increase in throughput for this specific case.

**Source:** [GitHub Issue - iree-org/iree #22309](https://github.com/iree-org/iree/issues/22309)

# High-Performance GEMM Kernel Technical Details for MI355X

## 1. MFMA Instructions for FP8

The article uses **`16x16x128` MFMA with FP8 inputs and FP32 accumulation**. The document also mentions that CDNA4 "adds V_MFMA_SCALE_F32_16X16X128_F8F6F4 and V_MFMA_SCALE_F32_32X32X64_F8F6F4" block-scaled variants.

## 2. Tile Sizes

The optimized configuration uses:
- **Output tile: 256×256**
- **K-dimension tile: 128**
- **Threads per block: 512**
- **Waves per block: 8**

The document notes this "256x256_t512" variant achieved the "highest-performing kernel tested."

## 3. 8-Wave Ping-Pong Algorithm

The pattern employs "eight waves per thread block with two waves resident per SIMD." Key mechanism:

> "After reaching barrier 0, waves 4, 5, 6, and 7 stall, while waves 0, 1, 2, and 3 continue executing code block 1. When waves 0, 1, 2, and 3 reach barrier 1, they release waves 4, 5, 6, and 7."

This alternates memory and compute instructions between wave pairs using `__builtin_amdgcn_s_barrier()`, `__builtin_amdgcn_s_setprio()`, and `__builtin_amdgcn_sched_barrier()`.

## 4. LDS Swizzling

The technique uses "a row-based XOR remap on 16-byte columns" to eliminate bank conflicts:

```c
int swizzle_col(int row, int col) {
    const int pair = (row >> 1) & 7;
    const int perm = pair ^ (((pair >> 1) ^ (pair >> 2)) & 1);
    const int mask = perm << 4;
    return col ^ mask;
}
```

This redistributes lane accesses across the 64 LDS banks to prevent conflicts during `ds_read_b128` operations.

## 5. Compilation Flags

The article does not specify explicit compiler flags. It references using HIP/C++ with inline assembly and LLVM intrinsics but provides no makefile or cmake configuration details.

## 6. Performance Results

For **M=N=K=4096**:
- **8-Wave kernel: 2680.33 TFLOPS/s** (0.0512 ms)
- **hipBLASLt baseline: 2750.42 TFLOPS/s** (0.04997 ms)
- **Gap: ~2.5%** below reference

For **M=N=K=8192**:
- **8-Wave kernel: 3204.15 TFLOPS/s**
- **hipBLASLt: 3130.21 TFLOPS/s**
- **Advantage: ~2.4% above** reference

## 7. Kernel Structure (Pseudocode)

The hot loop uses double buffering with alternating LDS slots:

```c
#pragma unroll 2
for (int k=0; k<K/128 - 2; k+=1; tic^=1, toc^=1) {
    // Wave 0-3: issue async loads (vmem/LDS)
    issue async ds_read_b128 reads: B_lds[tic][0] -> b_reg0;
    issue async buffer loads: vmem -> A_lds[toc][1];
    
    // Wave 4-7: execute MFMA
    __builtin_amdgcn_s_waitcnt(lgkmcnt(0));
    __builtin_amdgcn_s_setprio(1);
    c_reg0 += mma(a_reg, b_reg0);  // Matrix Core op
    __builtin_amdgcn_s_setprio(0);
    
    // Swap and repeat
}
```

The prologue prefetches the first tile; the epilogue manually unrolls final K iterations to drain in-flight memory requests.

     2→"""Continuous Evolution Pipeline for AMD MI355X Speedrun.

     4→This script implements a continuous loop:
     5→1. Mutate/Refine kernels based on latest research (MXFP4, MLA, MoE).

     7→3. Only submit to the leaderboard if the benchmark score is strictly better
     8→   than our current best recorded time.
     9→"""

    43→        with open(STATE_FILE, "r") as f:
    44→            return json.load(f)

    51→def extract_time(output):
    52→    """Extract performance time in microseconds from runner output."""
    53→    match = re.search(r"Performance:\s+([0-9.]+)\s+us", output)
    54→    if match:
    55→        return float(match.group(1))

    58→def submit(kernel, path, mode="benchmark"):
    59→    file_path = Path(path)
    60→    if not file_path.exists():
    61→        print(f"[{datetime.now().isoformat()}] ERROR: {path} not found!")
    62→        return None
    63→        
    64→    print(f"[{datetime.now().isoformat()}] Submitting {kernel} in {mode} mode...")
    65→    cmd = [

    67→        "--mode", mode,
    68→        "--gpu", "MI355X",
    69→        "--leaderboard", f"amd-{kernel}",
    70→        "--no-tui"
    71→    ]
    72→    
    73→    try:
    74→        res = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=300)
    75→        if res.returncode == 0:
    76→            print(f"[{datetime.now().isoformat()}] ✓ {kernel} {mode} SUCCESSFUL")
    77→            if mode == "benchmark":
    78→                time_us = extract_time(res.stdout)
    79→                if time_us is not None:
    80→                    print(f"[{datetime.now().isoformat()}]   Result: {time_us} us")
    81→                    return time_us
    82→            return True
    83→        else:
    84→            print(f"[{datetime.now().isoformat()}] ✗ {kernel} {mode} FAILED: {res.stderr[:200]}")
    85→            return None
    86→    except Exception as e:
    87→        print(f"[{datetime.now().isoformat()}] ! {kernel} {mode} EXCEPTION: {e}")
    88→        return None

    95→    # This is where we integrate gpu_kernel_scientist.py or custom AST modifications.

    99→def continuous_loop():

   101→    state = load_state()
   102→    
   103→    while True:

   105→        
   106→        for kernel, config in state.items():
   107→            path = config["path"]

   110→            # Step 1: Benchmark

   115→                time.sleep(60)
   116→                continue
   117→
   118→            print(f"Waiting {RATE_LIMIT}s for rate limit...")
   119→            time.sleep(RATE_LIMIT)
   120→            
   121→            # Step 2: Conditional Leaderboard Submission
   122→            if new_time is not None and new_time < best_time:
   123→                print(f"[{datetime.now().isoformat()}] *** BREAKTHROUGH! {new_time} us is better than {best_time} us ***")
   124→                success = submit(kernel, path, mode="leaderboard")
   125→                if success:

   127→                    save_state(state)
   128→                print(f"Waiting {RATE_LIMIT}s for rate limit...")
   129→                time.sleep(RATE_LIMIT)
   130→            elif new_time is not None:
   131→                print(f"[{datetime.now().isoformat()}] No improvement ({new_time} us >= {best_time} us). Skipping submission.")
   132→            
   133→if __name__ == "__main__":
   134→    continuous_loop()

     1→"""K-Search tree for adaptive kernel optimization strategy exploration."""
     2→
     3→from __future__ import annotations
     4→
     5→import json
     6→import uuid
     7→from dataclasses import dataclass, field
     8→from datetime import datetime, timezone
     9→from enum import Enum
    10→from pathlib import Path
    11→from typing import Any
    12→
    13→
    14→class NodeStatus(str, Enum):
    15→    OPEN = "OPEN"
    16→    CLOSED = "CLOSED"
    17→    DIVERGED = "DIVERGED"
    18→
    19→
    20→KERNEL_BASE_K: dict[str, int] = {
    21→    "mla": 12,
    22→    "moe": 8,
    23→    "gemm": 7,
    24→}
    25→
    26→MIN_K = 3
    27→
    28→
    29→@dataclass
    30→class KNode:
    31→    id: str
    32→    parent_id: str | None
    33→    strategy: str
    34→    status: NodeStatus
    35→    v_score: float
    36→    depth: int
    37→    attempt_history: list[dict[str, Any]] = field(default_factory=list)
    38→    children: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    39→    kernel_type: str = "gemm"
    40→    meta_prompt: str | None = None
    41→
    42→    @property
    43→    def best_score(self) -> float:
    44→        if not self.attempt_history:
    45→            return 0.0
    46→        return max(a["score"] for a in self.attempt_history)
    47→
    48→    @property
    49→    def success_rate(self) -> float:
    50→        """Fraction of attempts with score > 0.5."""
    51→        if not self.attempt_history:
    52→            return 0.0
    53→        successes = sum(1 for a in self.attempt_history if a["score"] > 0.5)
    54→        return successes / len(self.attempt_history)
    55→
    56→    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
    57→        return {
    58→            "id": self.id,
    59→            "parent_id": self.parent_id,
    60→            "strategy": self.strategy,
    61→            "status": self.status.value,
    62→            "v_score": self.v_score,
    63→            "depth": self.depth,
    64→            "attempt_history": self.attempt_history,
    65→            "children": self.children,
    66→            "kernel_type": self.kernel_type,
    67→            "meta_prompt": self.meta_prompt,
    68→        }
    69→
    70→    @classmethod
    71→    def from_dict(cls, data: dict[str, Any]) -> KNode:
    72→        return cls(
    73→            id=data["id"],
    74→            parent_id=data.get("parent_id"),
    75→            strategy=data["strategy"],
    76→            status=NodeStatus(data["status"]),
    77→            v_score=data["v_score"],
    78→            depth=data["depth"],
    79→            attempt_history=data.get("attempt_history", []),
    80→            children=data.get("children", []),
    81→            kernel_type=data.get("kernel_type", "gemm"),
    82→            meta_prompt=data.get("meta_prompt"),
    83→        )
    84→
    85→
    86→class KSearchTree:
    87→
    88→    def __init__(self, kernel_type: str) -> None:
    89→        if kernel_type not in KERNEL_BASE_K:
    90→            raise ValueError(
    91→                f"kernel_type must be one of {list(KERNEL_BASE_K)}, got {kernel_type!r}"
    92→            )
    93→        self.kernel_type = kernel_type
    94→        self.nodes: dict[str, KNode] = {}
    95→
    96→    def _gen_id(self) -> str:
    97→        return uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]
    98→
    99→    def insert_child(
   100→        self,
   101→        parent_id: str | None,
   102→        strategy: str,
   103→        v_score: float,
   104→        meta_prompt: str | None = None,
   105→    ) -> KNode:
   106→        """Add a child node under *parent_id* (None for root-level nodes)."""
   107→        depth = 0
   108→        if parent_id is not None:
   109→            parent = self.nodes.get(parent_id)
   110→            if parent is None:
   111→                raise KeyError(f"Parent node {parent_id!r} not found")
   112→            depth = parent.depth + 1
   113→
   114→        node = KNode(
   115→            id=self._gen_id(),
   116→            parent_id=parent_id,
   117→            strategy=strategy,
   118→            status=NodeStatus.OPEN,
   119→            v_score=max(0.0, min(1.0, v_score)),
   120→            depth=depth,
   121→            kernel_type=self.kernel_type,
   122→            meta_prompt=meta_prompt,
   123→        )
   124→        self.nodes[node.id] = node
   125→
   126→        if parent_id is not None:
   127→            self.nodes[parent_id].children.append(node.id)
   128→
   129→        return node
   130→
   131→    def select_best(self) -> KNode:
   132→        """Return the highest V-score OPEN frontier node.
   133→
   134→        Raises ValueError when no OPEN nodes exist.
   135→        """
   136→        open_nodes = [n for n in self.nodes.values() if n.status == NodeStatus.OPEN]
   137→        if not open_nodes:
   138→            raise ValueError("No OPEN nodes in tree")
   139→        return max(open_nodes, key=lambda n: n.v_score)
   140→    _STAGNATION_WINDOW = 5
   141→    _STAGNATION_DELTA = 0.02
   142→
   143→    def record_attempt(self, node_id: str, code: str, score: float) -> None:
   144→        """Append an attempt and check for stagnation."""
   145→        node = self.nodes[node_id]
   146→        node.attempt_history.append(
   147→            {
   148→                "code": code,
   149→                "score": score,
   150→                "timestamp": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
   151→            }
   152→        )
   153→        node.v_score = max(node.v_score, score)
   154→
   155→        # Stagnation: last N attempts show no meaningful improvement
   156→        recent = node.attempt_history[-self._STAGNATION_WINDOW :]
   157→        if len(recent) >= self._STAGNATION_WINDOW:
   158→            scores = [a["score"] for a in recent]
   159→            if max(scores) - min(scores) < self._STAGNATION_DELTA:
   160→                self.prune_node(node_id)
   161→
   162→    def adaptive_k(self, node: KNode) -> int:
   163→        """Compute branching factor K for *node*.
   164→
   165→        K = base(kernel) - depth + parent_bonus, clamped to [MIN_K, base].
   166→        """
   167→        base = KERNEL_BASE_K[self.kernel_type]
   168→        k = base - node.depth
   169→
   170→        # Parent success bonus
   171→        if node.parent_id is not None:
   172→            parent = self.nodes.get(node.parent_id)
   173→            if parent is not None and parent.success_rate > 0.5:
   174→                k += 2
   175→
   176→        return max(MIN_K, min(k, base + 2))
   177→
   178→    def check_divergence(self, node: KNode, score: float) -> bool:
   179→        """True when *score* is significantly worse than the node's best."""
   180→        best = node.best_score
   181→        if best == 0.0:
   182→            return False
   183→        return score < 0.8 * best
   184→
   185→    def apply_evolution(self, results: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> None:
   186→        """Process a batch of evolution operations.
   187→
   188→        Each result dict must have an ``"op"`` key:
   189→        - ``INSERT``: requires ``parent_id``, ``strategy``, ``v_score``
   190→        - ``UPDATE``: requires ``node_id``, ``code``, ``score``
   191→        - ``PRUNE``:  requires ``node_id``
   192→        """
   193→        for r in results:
   194→            op = r["op"]
   195→            if op == "INSERT":
   196→                self.insert_child(r["parent_id"], r["strategy"], r["v_score"])
   197→            elif op == "UPDATE":
   198→                self.record_attempt(r["node_id"], r["code"], r["score"])
   199→            elif op == "PRUNE":
   200→                self.prune_node(r["node_id"])
   201→            else:
   202→                raise ValueError(f"Unknown evolution op: {op!r}")
   203→
   204→    def prune_node(self, node_id: str) -> None:
   205→        """Mark a node CLOSED (exhausted, stagnant)."""
   206→        self.nodes[node_id].status = NodeStatus.CLOSED
   207→
   208→    def diverge_node(self, node_id: str) -> None:
   209→        """Mark a node DIVERGED for cross-kernel learning."""
   210→        self.nodes[node_id].status = NodeStatus.DIVERGED
   211→
   212→    def get_cross_kernel_failures(self) -> list[str]:
   213→        """Return strategies of DIVERGED nodes (share with other kernels)."""
   214→        return [
   215→            n.strategy
   216→            for n in self.nodes.values()
   217→            if n.status == NodeStatus.DIVERGED
   218→        ]
   219→
   220→    def get_cross_kernel_successes(self) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
   221→        """Return strategies whose best score exceeds 0.8."""
   222→        out: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
   223→        for n in self.nodes.values():
   224→            if n.best_score > 0.8:
   225→                out.append(
   226→                    {
   227→                        "strategy": n.strategy,
   228→                        "best_score": n.best_score,
   229→                        "kernel_type": n.kernel_type,
   230→                        "depth": n.depth,
   231→                    }
   232→                )
   233→        return out
   234→
   235→    def save(self, path: str | Path) -> None:
   236→        """Persist tree to JSON."""
   237→        payload = {
   238→            "kernel_type": self.kernel_type,
   239→            "nodes": {nid: n.to_dict() for nid, n in self.nodes.items()},
   240→        }
   241→        p = Path(path)
   242→        p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
   243→        p.write_text(json.dumps(payload, indent=2))
   244→
   245→    @classmethod
   246→    def load(cls, path: str | Path) -> KSearchTree:
   247→        """Restore tree from JSON."""
   248→        data = json.loads(Path(path).read_text())
   249→        tree = cls(kernel_type=data["kernel_type"])
   250→        for nid, ndata in data["nodes"].items():
   251→            tree.nodes[nid] = KNode.from_dict(ndata)
   252→        return tree
   253→
   254→    def summary(self) -> str:
   255→        open_ct = sum(1 for n in self.nodes.values() if n.status == NodeStatus.OPEN)
   256→        closed_ct = sum(1 for n in self.nodes.values() if n.status == NodeStatus.CLOSED)
   257→        div_ct = sum(1 for n in self.nodes.values() if n.status == NodeStatus.DIVERGED)
   258→        lines = [
   259→            f"KSearchTree(kernel={self.kernel_type}, nodes={len(self.nodes)}, "
   260→            f"open={open_ct}, closed={closed_ct}, diverged={div_ct})",
   261→        ]
   262→        for n in self.nodes.values():
   263→            indent = "  " * n.depth
   264→            lines.append(
   265→                f"  {indent}[{n.status.value:>8}] {n.strategy}  "
   266→                f"v={n.v_score:.3f}  attempts={len(n.attempt_history)}  "
   267→                f"K={self.adaptive_k(n)}"
   268→            )
   269→        return "\n".join(lines)
   270→
   271→if __name__ == "__main__":
   272→    tree = KSearchTree("moe")
   273→
   274→    # Root-level strategies
   275→    a = tree.insert_child(None, "split_experts_v1", 0.65)
   276→    b = tree.insert_child(None, "fused_gate_topk", 0.72)
   277→    c = tree.insert_child(None, "shared_expert_reuse", 0.58)
   278→
   279→    # Record some attempts
   280→    tree.record_attempt(a.id, "# split impl v1\n...", 0.67)
   281→    tree.record_attempt(b.id, "# fused gate v1\n...", 0.74)
   282→    tree.record_attempt(b.id, "# fused gate v2\n...", 0.81)
   283→    tree.record_attempt(c.id, "# shared reuse v1\n...", 0.60)
   284→    tree.record_attempt(c.id, "# shared reuse v2\n...", 0.35)
   285→
   286→    # Divergence: c's latest score dropped well below its best (0.35 < 0.8 * 0.60)
   287→    if tree.check_divergence(c, 0.35):
   288→        tree.diverge_node(c.id)
   289→
   290→    # Expand best node
   291→    best = tree.select_best()
   292→    k = tree.adaptive_k(best)
   293→    tree.insert_child(best.id, f"{best.strategy}__refine_tiling", 0.78)
   294→    tree.insert_child(best.id, f"{best.strategy}__warp_shuffle", 0.75)
   295→
   296→    print(tree.summary())
   297→    print()
   298→    print(f"Adaptive K for best node ({best.strategy}): {k}")
   299→    print(f"Cross-kernel failures: {tree.get_cross_kernel_failures()}")
   300→    print(f"Cross-kernel successes: {tree.get_cross_kernel_successes()}")

## V-JEPA 2.1: Unlocking Dense Features in Video Self-Supervised Learning

The paper was submitted on March 15, 2026, and last revised on March 17, 2026 (v2). The authors are from FAIR at Meta and Universidad de Zaragoza, including Lorenzo Mur-Labadia, Matthew Muckley, Amir Bar, Mido Assran, Koustuv Sinha, Mike Rabbat, Yann LeCun, Nicolas Ballas, and Adrien Bardes.

### Overview

V-JEPA 2.1 is a family of self-supervised models that learn dense, high-quality visual representations for both images and videos while retaining strong global scene understanding.

### Four Key Components

1. **Dense Predictive Loss**: A dense predictive loss uses a masking-based objective in which both visible and masked tokens contribute to the training signal, encouraging explicit spatial and temporal grounding. Unlike V-JEPA 2, which restricts supervision to masked regions, the loss is applied to both masked (prediction) and unmasked (context) tokens.

2. **Deep Self-Supervision**: Deep self-supervision applies the self-supervised objective hierarchically across multiple intermediate encoder layers to improve representation quality.

3. **Multi-Modal Tokenizers**: Multi-modal tokenizers enable unified training across images and videos.

4. **Effective Scaling**: The model benefits from effective scaling in both model capacity and training data.

### Why It Matters

The authors identify the root cause of the bottleneck in prior JEPA iterations: the training loss was applied exclusively to masked regions, meaning unmasked context patches were under no pressure to retain local spatial fidelity, effectively degenerating into global aggregators similar to register tokens, which compromised dense feature map quality.

### Results

V-JEPA 2.1 achieves state-of-the-art performance on several challenging benchmarks, including 7.71 mAP on Ego4D for short-term object-interaction anticipation and 40.8 Recall@5 on EPIC-KITCHENS for high-level action anticipation, as well as a 20-point improvement in real-robot grasping success rate over V-JEPA-2 AC.

The model also demonstrates strong performance in robotic navigation (5.687 ATE on TartanDrive), depth estimation (0.307 RMSE on NYUv2 with a linear probe), and global recognition (77.7 on Something-Something-V2).

### Resources

- **arXiv**: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14482](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14482)
- **Code & Models**: [https://github.com/facebookresearch/vjepa2](https://github.com/facebookresearch/vjepa2)

## Paper Found: **"Enhance the Safety in Reinforcement Learning by ADRC Lagrangian Methods"**

**arXiv ID:** [2601.18142](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18142) (published January 26, 2026)

### Summary

Safe reinforcement learning (Safe RL) seeks to maximize rewards while satisfying safety constraints, typically addressed through Lagrangian-based methods. However, existing approaches, including PID and classical Lagrangian methods, suffer from oscillations and frequent safety violations due to parameter sensitivity and inherent phase lag.

To address these limitations, the authors propose ADRC-Lagrangian methods that leverage Active Disturbance Rejection Control (ADRC) for enhanced robustness and reduced oscillations. Their unified framework encompasses classical and PID Lagrangian methods as special cases while significantly improving safety performance.

### Key Results

Extensive experiments demonstrate that the approach reduces safety violations by up to **74%**, constraint violation magnitudes by **89%**, and average costs by **67%**, establishing superior effectiveness for Safe RL in complex environments.

### How It Works

Unlike classical adaptive methods that often require a parametric model or extensive gain tuning, ADRC treats all uncertainty—including model error, noise, and nonstationarity—as a lumped disturbance, and employs a lightweight observer to estimate and cancel it online.

The resulting method is simple to implement, model-free, and optimizer-agnostic. The authors also derive a theoretical lower bound on the observer gain that provides safe defaults across diverse environments and establish through frequency-domain analysis that their approach achieves smaller disturbance-estimation error and reduced phase lag.

### Additional Findings

- ADRC shows robustness to variations in its tuning parameters ($c_r, k_{ap}, k_{ad}$), outperforming baselines even with sub-optimal settings.
- ADRC-Lagrangian methods are shown to be universally applicable to various Lagrangian-based safe RL algorithms.
- Removing either the dynamic reference $r(t)$ or the dynamic weight (related to $\omega_o$) from the ADRC formulation leads to performance degradation, confirming the importance of both components.

The paper is also available on [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/forum?id=5coA0SxUua).

## Causal-JEPA: Learning World Models through Object-Level Latent Interventions

### Paper & Code
- **Paper:** [arXiv:2602.11389](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11389), submitted on Wed, 11 Feb 2026
- **Authors:** Heejeong Nam, Quentin Le Lidec, Lucas Maes, Yann LeCun, Randall Balestriero
- **Code:** The code is available at [https://github.com/galilai-group/cjepa](https://github.com/galilai-group/cjepa).
- **Model checkpoints** are also available on [Hugging Face (HazelNam/CJEPA)](https://huggingface.co/HazelNam/CJEPA).
- **Project page:** [https://hazel-heejeong-nam.github.io/cjepa/](https://hazel-heejeong-nam.github.io/cjepa/)

### What is C-JEPA?
C-JEPA is a simple and flexible object-centric world model that extends masked joint embedding prediction from image patches to object-centric representations. By applying object-level masking that requires an object's state to be inferred from other objects, C-JEPA induces latent interventions with counterfactual-like effects and prevents shortcut solutions, making interaction reasoning essential.

### Key Mechanism: Object-Level Masking
C-JEPA treats object masking as a structured latent intervention. By masking an object's trajectory throughout the history window (except for a minimal identity anchor), the model is forced to rely on interactions with other entities to minimize prediction error.

C-JEPA builds upon a two-stage framework: a frozen object-centric encoder (typically VideoSAUR or SAVi) that extracts object-level slot representations, and a ViT-style masked transformer predictor operating jointly on masked history and future slots. Object-level masking is applied such that selected object slots across the temporal history receive minimal identity anchors and are otherwise replaced by masked tokens. The predictor must reconstruct these masked object histories and forecast future object states.

### Key Results
- **Visual QA:** C-JEPA leads to consistent gains in visual question answering, with an absolute improvement of about 20% in counterfactual reasoning compared to the same architecture without object-level masking.
- **Planning Efficiency:** It matches the performance of DINO-WM while using only 1.02% of the total latent features, enabling 8x faster planning.
- **Push-T Control:** With four object slots and auxiliary action/proprioception embeddings, C-JEPA achieves 88.7% planning success versus 60.7% for OC-DINO-WM and 91.3% for DINO-WM, using only 1.02% of the input tokens.
- **Robustness:** C-JEPA achieves the strongest performance without relying on pixel-level reconstruction. Removing reconstruction leads to severe degradation in baselines like SlotFormer, whereas C-JEPA's masking-based objective remains highly effective.

### Code Repository Details
The GitHub repository ([galilai-group/cjepa](https://github.com/galilai-group/cjepa)) includes:

- The framework operates on a 128-dimensional latent slot space and trains efficiently on a single L40s GPU.

### Formal Analysis
The paper formally characterizes object-level masked prediction as a causal inductive bias, showing that latent interventions make interaction reasoning necessary for minimizing the training objective.

## Key Findings

### 1. **HipKittens – AITER Backend (HazyResearch)**
As of March 2026, HipKittens is officially an AITER backend, with the first HK kernels landing in AITER. The project provides Docker setup instructions for MI350X and MI355X with gfx950 architecture, using the `rocm7.0_preview_pytorch_training_mi35x_beta` Docker image.

### 2. **JAX-AITER (ROCm)**
JAX-AITER supports FP8 block-scale for gfx950 only. The setup involves setting `GPU_ARCHS=gfx950` — "gfx942 for MI300, gfx950 for MI350." It supports BF16 GEMM using "AITER hand-tuned ASM kernels" with bf16 inputs, bf16 output, and custom_vjp for training.

### 3. **ROCm/AITER Releases**
Recent AITER releases include FMHA BWD optimizations for D48 for GFX950, Triton FP4 fusion for the 355, and various kernel naming and CI improvements.

### 4. **GPU MODE Hackathon – AMD MI355X Kernel Optimization**
A GPU MODE Hackathon Phase 1 preparation guide describes three kernel optimization problems based on operations critical to DeepSeek-R1 model inference on AMD MI355X GPUs. The tasks include:
- Optimizing the attention mechanism for DeepSeek-R1's innovative MLA architecture during the decode (autoregressive) phase.
- Implementing a fused MoE (Mixture of Experts) layer with MXFP4 weight quantization, optimized for DeepSeek-R1's expert architecture.
- Implementing efficient MXFP4 quantized matrix multiplication: bf16 A × MXFP4 B → bf16 C.

The submission framework uses `submission.py` with custom kernels: evaluation is run via `python eval.py --problem mixed-mla --submission submission.py`, with `torch.cuda.synchronize()` used before and after timing the custom kernel call.

### 5. **SGLang + AITER on MI355X**
SGLang has been running on MI355X using the `rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.7-rocm700-mi35x-20260121` Docker image, with the AITER attention backend.

### 6. **Mini-SGLang AMD ROCm Support**
A March 2026 issue proposes adding AMD MI300X/MI355X GPU support to mini-SGLang, involving ~1,000-1,200 lines of changes across ~20 files, mainly replacing NVIDIA-specific utilities with PyTorch fallbacks or AMD equivalents (AITER/CK). This includes arch detection changes like `is_sm90_supported → is_gfx942/is_gfx950`.

### 7. **GFX950 and MI355X Background**
Phoronix suggests GFX950 is "likely the internal codename for the MI325X or MI350 (MI355X) accelerators - though the latter is more likely since the MI325X has been available since October." The MI355X is expected to deliver 9.2 PetaFLOPS of FP4 compute performance and features 288GB of HBM3E.

Here are the results for your search on **Safety-Gymnasium** and safe reinforcement learning:

## Safety-Gymnasium Overview

Safety-Gymnasium is an environment suite that encompasses safety-critical tasks in both single and multi-agent scenarios, accepting vector and vision-only input. It was presented at the 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.

### Motivation

AI systems possess significant potential to drive societal progress. However, their deployment often faces obstacles due to substantial safety concerns. Safe reinforcement learning (SafeRL) emerges as a solution to optimize policies while simultaneously adhering to multiple constraints, thereby addressing the challenge of integrating reinforcement learning in safety-critical scenarios.

### Key Components

- **Environments:** They designed a variety of safety-enhanced learning tasks and integrated contributions from the RL community: safety-velocity, safety-run, safety-circle, safety-goal, safety-button, etc.
- **Algorithms:** They offer a library of algorithms named Safe Policy Optimization (SafePO), comprising 16 state-of-the-art SafeRL algorithms.
- **Two environment types:** Environments are categorized into two primary types: Gymnasium-based, featuring agents of escalating complexity for algorithm verification and comparison, and Isaac-Gym-based, incorporating sophisticated agents that harness the parallel processing power of Isaac-Gym's GPU.

### Vision-Based Environments

To effectively evaluate vision-based safe reinforcement learning algorithms, they devised a more realistic visual environment utilizing MuJoCo. This enhanced environment facilitates the incorporation of both RGB and RGB-d inputs.

### Safety-DexterousHands

Safety-DexterousHands is a novel collection of learning environments built upon DexterousHands and the Isaac-Gym simulator engine. Leveraging GPU capabilities, it enables large-scale parallel sample collection, significantly accelerating the training process. The environments support both single-agent and multi-agent settings.

### GitHub & Installation

The project is hosted at [PKU-Alignment/safety-gymnasium on GitHub](https://github.com/PKU-Alignment/safety-gymnasium). They have updated the environments for both the Safe Vision series and the Safe Isaac Gym series. However, due to package size constraints, versions v1.1.0 and v1.2.0 have not yet been uploaded to PyPI, so users are required to manually download and install.

### HuggingFace – Related Work

While no direct HuggingFace × Safety-Gymnasium 2026 collaboration appeared in the results, a related project was found: HuggingFace's **gym-hil** is a collection of gymnasium environments for Human-In-the-Loop (HIL) reinforcement learning, compatible with Hugging Face's LeRobot codebase. During every rollout, the policy proposes an action, but the human may instantly override it; this approach improves sample efficiency and promotes safer exploration.

---

**Note:** The search did not surface any specific **2026 announcements** tying HuggingFace directly to new Safety-Gymnasium environments. The most relevant results are the existing Safety-Gymnasium benchmark (NeurIPS 2023) and HuggingFace's gym-hil project for safe human-in-the-loop RL.

We're using `at::cuda::getCurrentCUDAStream()` which should be the correct harness stream. The "work on another stream" error might be coming from the `dynamic_mxfp4_quant` call in the Python wrapper — that's an aiter function that might use its own stream internally.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Critical Runner Finding (L260):**
The "work on another stream" error from the runner's stream scanner likely fires because our `custom_kernel()` Python function calls `dynamic_mxfp4_quant()` (an aiter Triton kernel) AND our custom HIP kernel — the scanner detects HIP kernel launches on a stream that isn't the one it set up for timing. The reference `submission.py` avoids this because it only calls `aiter.gemm_a4w4()` which is a single well-known library call.

**Fix needed**: Either (a) ensure all GPU work stays on `torch.cuda.current_stream()`, or (b) use the reference submission's quantization path and only replace the GEMM compute, or (c) the issue is load_inline compilation itself creating a new context.

     1→# HipKittens + Native MXFP4 GEMM Spec for AMD MI355X (gfx950)
     2→
     3→**Status:** Research Complete
     4→**Date:** 2026-04-02
     5→**Target kernel:** `amd-mxfp4-mm`
     6→**Current time:** 22.8us (ranked) / 13.4us (ranked new shapes)
     7→**Leader:** 4.3us
     8→**Gap:** 3.1x - 5.3x
     9→**Strategy:** `load_inline` custom HIP kernel using native `__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_scale_f32` intrinsics
    10→
    11→---
    12→
    13→## Executive Summary
    14→
    15→The path to sub-10us MXFP4 GEMM on gfx950 is now clearly mapped:
    16→
    17→1. **HipKittens is NOT a drop-in header for load_inline.** It is compiled as a shared `.so` via a dedicated Makefile using PyBind11. The `#include <kittens.cuh>` pattern works inside `hipcc` compilation only, not via `torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline()`. HipKittens also does NOT have MXFP4/FP4 support in its current main branch (only BF16 and FP8).
    18→
    19→2. **The direct path to native MXFP4 GEMM on gfx950 is `__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_scale_f32_32x32x64_f8f6f4`.** This CDNA4-only intrinsic IS callable from `load_inline` HIP C++ kernels. It accepts FP4 (E2M1, Atype=4) inputs with per-tile E8M0 scales built into the instruction. No library needed.
    20→
    21→3. **The existing load_inline submissions are scalar fallback code** (fp4_to_f32 table lookup, one element per thread). They do not use MFMA hardware at all. Replacing them with a tiled MFMA kernel using the scaled MFMA intrinsic is the single highest-leverage change.
    22→
    23→---
    24→
    25→## 1. HipKittens: What It Is and Is NOT
    26→
    27→### What it provides (for BF16/FP8)
    28→
    29→**Repository:** https://github.com/HazyResearch/HipKittens
    30→**Paper:** arXiv:2511.08083 (Nov 2025)
    31→
    32→HipKittens is a C++ template DSL for AMD CDNA3/CDNA4 that wraps inline assembly into typed tile objects. Key components:
    33→
    34→**Tile type hierarchy:**
    35→```
    36→kittens/
    37→  include/
    38→    kittens.cuh          <- master include
    39→    common/
    40→      macros.cuh         <- inline asm wrappers: ds_read_b32, buffer_load_dwordx4, v_mfma_f32_*
    41→    types/
    42→      types.cuh          <- register/shared tile shapes

    76→
    77→### Why HipKittens is NOT usable via load_inline
    78→
    79→HipKittens compiles using `hipcc` via its own Makefile, linking PyBind11:
    80→```makefile
    81→ROCM_BUILD_DIR = /opt/rocm/bin
    82→HIP_COMPILER = $(ROCM_BUILD_DIR)/hipcc
    83→CFLAGS = -std=c++20 -w -shared -fPIC --offload-arch=gfx950
    84→INCLUDES = -I${THUNDERKITTENS_ROOT}/include -I/opt/rocm/include/hip
    85→```
    86→
    87→`torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline()` uses `clang++` (via `CXX="clang++"`) as the host compiler and invokes it with HIP offload arguments. The `kittens.cuh` header can in principle be included if:
    88→- `THUNDERKITTENS_ROOT` environment variable is set correctly
    89→- The header path is passed via `extra_cuda_cflags=["-I/path/to/HipKittens/include"]`
    90→- The runner has HipKittens cloned
    91→
    92→**Verdict:** HipKittens headers are NOT available on the Popcorn runner. They would need to be embedded inline or cloned at kernel build time. Even if available, they have no MXFP4 support.
    93→
    94→### What IS usable: The 8-Wave Ping-Pong Pattern
    95→
    96→The scheduling CONCEPT from HipKittens is directly implementable in a raw HIP kernel:
    97→
    98→```
    99→8-wave ping-pong (GEMM tile loop pattern):
   100→  - 8 waves per threadblock (WARPS_M=2, WARPS_N=4)
   101→  - Double-buffered shared memory: AS[2][2] and BS[2][2]
   102→  - tic/toc toggle: while waves[0..3] compute on AS[tic], waves[4..7] load into AS[toc]
   103→  - Roles swap each iteration via conditional barrier + sched_group_barrier
   104→  - Outer tile loop: prefetch tile[i+1] while computing tile[i]
   105→
   106→4-wave interleave (alternative for small M):
   107→  - 1 wave per SIMD, 4 waves total
   108→  - Each wave alternates small load+compute microbatches
   109→  - Better for memory-bound shapes (small M, large N/K)
   110→```
   111→
   112→**Key AMD-specific facts:**
   113→- HIPCC cannot allocate AGPRs as MFMA inputs/outputs — need `range<>` API (HipKittens) or inline assembly
   114→- For raw HIP kernels, use `__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_*` directly (avoids the AGPR allocation problem)
   115→- `__builtin_amdgcn_sched_barrier(mask)` and `__builtin_amdgcn_sched_group_barrier(mask, size, sync_id)` control instruction interleaving
   116→- `s_setprio` controls wave priority between compute and memory groups
   117→
   118→---

   125→#include <hip/hip_runtime.h>
   126→#include <hip/hip_ext_ocp.h>  // provides __amd_fp4x2_storage_t, __amd_extract_fp4, __amd_create_fp4x2
   127→
   128→// Two scaled MFMA variants for gfx950 CDNA4:
   129→// 16x16x128: output v4f32, input v8i32, C v4f32

   144→
   145→**Atype/Btype values:**
   146→- `0` = E4M3 (fp8)
   147→- `1` = E5M2 (bf8)
   148→- `2` = E2M3 (fp6)
   149→- `3` = E3M2 (bf6)

   152→**Scale semantics:** `scale_a` and `scale_b` are E8M0 bytes. Actual scale = `2^(scale_byte - 127)`. This matches the aiter `dynamic_mxfp4_quant` output format (E8M0 bytes before shuffle). Scale is applied INSIDE the MFMA instruction, after the dot product and before accumulation into `c_reg`.
   153→
   154→### Thread-to-Data Layout: 32x32x64 Tile
   155→
   156→For the 32x32x64 variant with a wave of 64 threads:
   157→
   158→```
   159→Per-thread ownership (wave64):
   160→  A tile (32 rows x 64 cols packed FP4):
   161→    - Threads 0..31:  rows 0..31, each thread holds 64 FP4 = 32 fp4x2 bytes
   162→    - Threads 32..63: rows 32..63 (second row-half — but 32x32 output, so rows 0..31 twice)
   163→
   164→  Actually for 32x32x64:
   165→    Each thread holds:
   166→      - a_reg: 32 FP4 elements (stored as 16 fp4x2 pairs in lower 128 bits of v8i32)
   167→      - b_reg: 32 FP4 elements (same format)
   168→      - scale_a: 1 E8M0 byte (uint8_t) — one scale covers 32 FP4 elements = 1 group
   169→      - scale_b: 1 E8M0 byte (uint8_t)
   170→      - c_reg:  16 FP32 values (output fragment)
   171→
   172→  FP4 packing type for input:
   173→    using fp4x2_t  = __amd_fp4x2_storage_t;     // uint8_t alias
   174→    using fp4x64_t = fp4x2_t __attribute__((ext_vector_type(32)));  // 256-bit vector, 64 fp4
   175→    // Upper 128 bits must be zero for MXFP4 mode
   176→```
   177→
   178→### Data Flow Diagram
   179→
   180→```
   181→Global Memory:
   182→  A_packed   [M, K//2] uint8  (FP4 pairs, row-major)
   183→  A_scale    [M, K//32] uint8 (E8M0 scale, row-major, 1 scale per 32 elements)
   184→  B_packed   [N, K//2] uint8  (B_shuffle from task input, pre-shuffled)
   185→  B_scale    [N, K//32] uint8 (B_scale_sh from task input, pre-shuffled)
   186→
   187→Shared Memory (double-buffered):
   188→  smem_A[2][BLOCK_M // 32][32 * 16] fp4x2_t   (two 32xK slices)
   189→  smem_B[2][BLOCK_N // 32][32 * 16] fp4x2_t   (two Kx32 slices)
   190→  smem_As[2][BLOCK_M] uint8                    (scales for A, one per row per group)
   191→  smem_Bs[2][BLOCK_N] uint8                    (scales for B, one per col per group)
   192→
   193→Register Tiles (per wave):
   194→  a_reg[16]  fp4x64_t  (loaded from smem_A, 64 fp4 per thread)
   195→  b_reg[16]  fp4x64_t  (loaded from smem_B)
   196→  scale_a    uint8_t   (loaded from smem_As)
   197→  scale_b    uint8_t   (loaded from smem_Bs)
   198→  c_accum[BLOCK_M//32][BLOCK_N//32] v16f32  (accumulated FP32 output)
   199→
   200→Output:
   201→  C [M, N] bfloat16 (converted from c_accum)
   202→```
   203→
   204→### Key Design Constraints
   205→
   206→**Scale granularity mismatch:** The hardware MFMA instruction takes ONE scale per operand per call. The competition task has scales at 32-element granularity (one E8M0 per 32 FP4 elements = one per 16 bytes packed). For a 32x32x64 tile:
   207→- K dimension is 64 FP4 elements = 2 scale groups (each 32 elements)

   205→
   206→**Scale granularity mismatch:** The hardware MFMA instruction takes ONE scale per operand per call. The competition task has scales at 32-element granularity (one E8M0 per 32 FP4 elements = one per 16 bytes packed). For a 32x32x64 tile:
   207→- K dimension is 64 FP4 elements = 2 scale groups (each 32 elements)
   208→- The MFMA covers 64 K elements in one call, but there are 2 different scales along K
   209→- **Solution:** Unroll the K loop by 2 (or 4) and call the MFMA once per scale group (32 elements = BLOCK_K=32 per MFMA call)
   210→
   211→**Tile sizing for competition shapes:**
   212→```
   213→Competition shapes:
   214→  M=4,   N=2880, K=512   -> K/32 = 16 scale groups per row
   215→  M=16,  N=2112, K=7168  -> K/32 = 224 scale groups per row  (BOTTLENECK)
   216→  M=32,  N=4096, K=512   -> K/32 = 16 groups
   217→  M=64,  N=7168, K=2048  -> K/32 = 64 groups
   218→  M=256, N=3072, K=1536  -> K/32 = 48 groups
   219→
   220→Recommended tile:
   221→  BLOCK_M = 32  (matches MFMA 32x32 tile)
   222→  BLOCK_N = 128 (4 MFMA tiles wide, good for wide N)
   223→  BLOCK_K = 32  (= 1 scale group, 1 MFMA call per K step)
   224→  WAVES_M = 1 (32 rows per wave)
   225→  WAVES_N = 4 (128/32 = 4 waves along N)
   226→  Total waves per block = 4
   227→```
   228→
   229→**For small M (M=4, M=16):** The MFMA tile is 32x32 minimum. For M<32, options:
   230→1. Pad M dimension to 32 (wastes compute on M=4: 8x waste)
   231→2. Use the 16x16x128 variant: smaller output tile, better for small M
   232→3. Fall back to aiter `gemm_a4w4` for shapes where BLOCK_M > M (and M is small)
   233→
   234→### Compilation Flags for load_inline
   235→
   236→```python
   237→extra_cuda_cflags=[
   238→    "--offload-arch=gfx950",
   239→    "-std=c++20",
   240→    "-O3",
   241→    "-w",                          # suppress warnings
   242→    "-DAMD_MFMA_SCALE_AVAILABLE",  # guard for gfx950-only code
   243→]
   244→```
   245→
   246→The `hip/hip_ext_ocp.h` header provides:
   247→- `__amd_fp4x2_storage_t` (uint8_t)
   248→- `__amd_extract_fp4(packed, index)` — extract nibble 0 or 1
   249→- `__amd_create_fp4x2(lo, hi)` — pack two nibbles
   250→
   251→This header is available in ROCm 7.0+.

   254→
   255→## 3. The Quant Bottleneck Still Applies
   256→
   257→The existing architecture calls `dynamic_mxfp4_quant(A)` for ~26-80us before ANY GEMM. This is still the dominant cost at Python dispatch level. The native MFMA kernel does NOT help with the quant cost.
   258→
   259→**BUT** there is now a credible path to eliminate quant dispatch by fusing it into the MFMA kernel:
   260→
   261→```
   262→Fused kernel architecture:
   263→  Thread block loads A [BLOCK_M rows, BLOCK_K elements] from global (bf16)
   264→  Computes MXFP4 quantization inline (max per group-of-32, E8M0 encoding)
```

### Step 2: GEMM v5 — MFMA Intrinsic Kernel
Write the kernel using hardware MFMA scaled instructions. ONE kernel, tested incrementally.

- [ ] Create `submission_mfma_native.py` with `__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_scale_f32_32x32x64_f8f6f4`
- [ ] Step 2a: Minimal MFMA proof — single tile (32×32×32), no tiling loop, hardcoded shapes
  - Verify: `popcorn --mode test` passes correctness
- [ ] Step 2b: Add K-dimension loop with scale-group alignment (BLOCK_K=32 = 1 scale group per MFMA)
  - Verify: passes on all 5 competition shapes
- [ ] Step 2c: Add M/N tiling (BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_N=128, 4 waves)
  - Verify: `popcorn --mode benchmark` — record time
- [ ] Step 2d: Double-buffered LDS for A and B tiles
  - Verify: benchmark improvement over 2c
- [ ] Step 2e: Submit to leaderboard if <15µs (any improvement over 22.8µs)

**Spec:** `research/challenges/luma_amd_speedrun/autoresearch/probes/hipkittens_mxfp4_gemm_spec.md`
**Key intrinsic:**
```cpp
#include <hip/hip_ext_ocp.h>
d = __builtin_amdgcn_mfma_scale_f32_32x32x64_f8f6f4(
    a_reg, b_reg, c_reg,
    4, 4,              // Atype=Btype=E2M1 (MXFP4)
    0, scale_a,        // E8M0 byte
    0, scale_b
);
```
**Tile sizing:** BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=32 (1 scale group), 4 waves per block
**Small-M handling:** For M<32, use 16x16x128 variant or fall back to aiter

### Step 3: Fuse A Quantization (if Step 2 works)
The quant overhead (~26µs) dominates. Fuse bf16→MXFP4 conversion into the GEMM kernel.

- [ ] Inline quantization: load A as bf16 → compute max per 32-element group → encode E8M0 scale → pack to FP4 → feed to MFMA
- [ ] This eliminates the Python `dynamic_mxfp4_quant` dispatch entirely

## Phase 4: Benchmark-Driven Learning Loop (Maximize Learning Between Submissions)

**Key constraint**: 1 real leaderboard submission per kernel per hour. But `--mode benchmark` and `--mode test` have NO rate limit. Every hour between submissions is learning time.

### 4.0 The Learning Loop (runs continuously)
```
Every 5 minutes:
  1. K-Search tree selects next mutation (load_inline variant)
  2. Generate kernel code via mutation
  3. popcorn --mode test (correctness check, ~30s)
  4. If correct: popcorn --mode benchmark (performance, ~60s)
  5. Record result to SurrealDB kernel_run table
  6. Update K-Search tree node score
  7. If benchmark < current_best: FLAG for leaderboard submission

Every 60 minutes:
  8. Submit best-of-hour to leaderboard (--mode leaderboard)
  9. Compare leaderboard rank vs benchmark estimate
  10. Update world model (benchmark→leaderboard correlation)
  11. SkillRefiner updates kernel PRIME skill with new finding
```

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Critical Discovery: `load_inline` compilation ITSELF triggers the stream error.**
The minimal test doesn't even call the compiled module — `custom_kernel()` only uses aiter. But the `load_inline()` call at module import time spawns `hipcc` compilation which creates a HIP context/stream as a side effect. The runner's stream scanner detects this during the import phase, before `custom_kernel()` is ever called.

**This means load_inline compilation must be deferred or avoided entirely.** The runner scans for stream violations at module import time, not just during kernel execution.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

This changes everything. Let me test if we can defer the compilation to inside `custom_kernel()`:

> AGENT

The pure aiter submission WORKS — it compiles the JIT modules and loads the pre-compiled `.co` kernels successfully. This confirms: **`load_inline` is the problem, not HIP kernel launches in general.** The aiter JIT system uses `hipModuleLoad` (loading pre-compiled kernels) which works fine. `load_inline` uses `hipcc` subprocess compilation which creates a conflicting HIP context.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**The Stream Mystery Solved (L264):**
1. **aiter JIT works**: It loads pre-compiled `.co` files via `hipModuleLoad` + `hipModuleGetFunction`. These route through the correct stream because they're loaded into the existing HIP context.
2. **load_inline is blocked**: It spawns `hipcc` (a subprocess) which initializes its OWN HIP context during compilation. This new context creates a new default stream. The runner's scanner detects this as "work on another stream."
3. **The path forward**: Instead of compiling HIP C++ at runtime via load_inline, we need to either (a) use aiter's existing pre-compiled `.co` kernel files, or (b) find a way to compile without creating a new HIP context, or (c) use `torch.cuda._compile_kernel()` (the experimental HIPRTC API from the research that may avoid context creation).
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Unfortunately, I was unable to find the specific issue you're looking for across multiple search attempts. Here's a summary of what I did find that's related:

### What I Found

1. **gpu-mode/popcorn-cli** is a CLI tool for the GPU MODE leaderboard competition platform. If you want to submit native CUDA code, you can use PyTorch's `load_inline` feature (which uses nvcc) or the more experimental `compile_kernel` API for fast compilation.

2. **`torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline()`** is PyTorch's JIT compilation mechanism for CUDA/C++ extensions. The simplest way to add a custom CUDA extension in PyTorch is `torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline()` — it expects both CUDA host and device code as strings and codegenerates a cpp extension by using `torch/extension.h`. From a UX perspective `load_inline()` is great but customers have complained of long compile times on the order of 90s for toy kernels.

3. **A newer alternative**: A more recent PR #151484 is proposing a new function `torch.cuda._compile_kernel()` and by leveraging nvrtc under the hood it can bring down compilation times to 0.01s!

### What I Couldn't Find

The specific error message containing **"work on another stream"** in the context of `load_inline` with gpu-mode/popcorn-cli, or any associated fix/workaround from 2026, did not appear in any search results. This could be because:

- It may be a very recent issue that hasn't been indexed yet.
- The exact phrasing may differ from what was searched.

# CUDA Inline Submission Analysis

## Compilation Approach

This example uses `torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline()` to compile CUDA code at runtime. The source is divided into:

- **CUDA source**: Contains the `add_kernel` template and `add_cuda` wrapper function
- **C++ source**: Provides the torch extension declaration

The compilation happens automatically when the module is loaded, with `verbose=True` enabling detailed output.

## Kernel Launch Details

The kernel launches use basic parameters:
- **Threads per block**: 256
- **Block count**: `(N + threads - 1) / threads` (standard grid calculation)
- **Syntax**: `add_kernel<scalar_t><<<blocks, threads>>>(...)` 

No explicit stream handling or special CUDA flags are visible in the code.

## Type Handling

The code leverages `AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES_AND_HALF()` to instantiate the template for supported floating-point types (float32, float64, float16), avoiding explicit type specialization.

## Error Checking

Post-launch error detection occurs via `cudaGetLastError()`, with exceptions thrown if kernel execution fails.

"""Test: Does the runner scan the SOURCE for 'load_inline' text?

This file contains the STRING "load_inline" in comments but does NOT
import or call it. If this ALSO fails, the runner does source scanning.
"""

# NOTE: torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline is NOT imported here

import aiter
from aiter import dtypes
from aiter.ops.triton.quant import dynamic_mxfp4_quant
from aiter.utility.fp4_utils import e8m0_shuffle
from task import input_t, output_t


def custom_kernel(data: input_t) -> output_t:
    """Pure aiter GEMM — no load_inline anywhere."""
    A, B, B_q, B_shuffle, B_scale_sh = data

    A_q, A_scale_e8m0 = dynamic_mxfp4_quant(A.contiguous())
    A_scale_sh = e8m0_shuffle(A_scale_e8m0).view(dtypes.fp8_e8m0)
    A_q = A_q.view(dtypes.fp4x2)
    return aiter.gemm_a4w4(
        A_q, B_shuffle, A_scale_sh, B_scale_sh,
        dtype=dtypes.bf16, bpreshuffle=True,
    )
```

  "content": "\"\"\"MXFP4 GEMM — try tritonblas.matmul_fp4 path.\n\nFrom tritonblas-matmul-fp4-api skill:\n- All tensors MUST be torch.uint8 views\n- B layout is [N, K//2] row-major (NOT transposed like aiter)\n- Output C must be pre-allocated and passed as 3rd positional argument\n- Uses Triton JIT under the hood — may be faster for some shapes\n\"\"\"\n\nimport torch\n\nfrom task import input_t, output_t\n\n\ndef custom_kernel(data: input_t) -> output_t:\n    A, B, B_q, B_shuffle, B_scale_sh = data\n    m, k = A.shape\n    n = B.shape[0]\n\n    try:\n        from aiter.ops.triton.quant import dynamic_mxfp4_quant\n        from aiter.utility.fp4_utils import e8m0_shuffle\n        from tritonblas import matmul_fp4\n\n        # Quantize A\n        A_q, A_scale = dynamic_mxfp4_quant(A.contiguous())\n\n        # tritonblas needs uint8 views, un-shuffled\n        A_packed = A_q.view(torch.uint8)\n        A_scale_bytes = A_scale.view(torch.uint8)\n\n        # B_q is already [N, K/2] from generate_input\n        B_packed = B_q.view(torch.uint8)\n\n        # Need un-shuffled B scale — re-quantize B to get it\n        _, B_scale_raw = dynamic_mxfp4_quant(B.contiguous())\n        B_scale_bytes = B_scale_raw.view(torch.uint8)\n\n        # Pre-allocate output\n        C = torch.empty((m, n), dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=A.device)\n\n        # tritonblas matmul_fp4: (A, B, C, A_scale, B_scale)\n        matmul_fp4(A_packed, B_packed, C, A_scale_bytes, B_scale_bytes)\n        return C\n\n    except Exception as e:\n        # Fallback to aiter\n        import aiter\n        from aiter import dtypes\n\n        A_q, A_scale = dynamic_mxfp4_quant(A.contiguous())\n        A_scale_sh = e8m0_shuffle(A_scale).view(dtypes.fp8_e8m0)\n        A_q = A_q.view(dtypes.fp4x2)\n        return aiter.gemm_a4w4(\n            A_q, B_shuffle, A_scale_sh, B_scale_sh,\n            dtype=dtypes.bf16, bpreshuffle=True,\n        )\n"

> AGENT

Mixed results! The tritonblas path is FASTER for some shapes (16.7µs vs 19.5µs for small shapes) but MUCH WORSE for M=16,K=7168 (66µs vs 33µs). The re-quant of B is killing performance on large shapes.

The problem is we're re-quantizing B from bf16, but B is already quantized. We need to use B_q directly. But tritonblas needs un-shuffled B — and we only have B_shuffle (aiter shuffled format).

Let me try a hybrid: use tritonblas for small shapes, aiter for large:

> TOOL

{
  "file_path": "/home/mike-anderson/dev/cohezion/luma_speedrun/amd-mxfp4-mm/submission_hybrid.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"MXFP4 GEMM — hybrid aiter path with shape-aware dispatch.\n\nUse aiter gemm_a4w4 for all shapes (proven fastest overall).\nSkip .contiguous() since A comes from generate_input already contiguous.\nUse @torch.no_grad() to skip autograd.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport torch\nimport aiter\nfrom aiter import dtypes\nfrom aiter.ops.triton.quant import dynamic_mxfp4_quant\nfrom aiter.utility.fp4_utils import e8m0_shuffle\nfrom task import input_t, output_t\n\n\n@torch.no_grad()\ndef custom_kernel(data: input_t) -> output_t:\n    A, B, B_q, B_shuffle, B_scale_sh = data\n\n    # Quantize A — this is the bottleneck (~12-15µs)\n    A_q, A_scale = dynamic_mxfp4_quant(A)\n    A_scale_sh = e8m0_shuffle(A_scale).view(dtypes.fp8_e8m0)\n    A_q = A_q.view(dtypes.fp4x2)\n\n    # aiter ASM path — fastest for all shapes\n    return aiter.gemm_a4w4(\n        A_q, B_shuffle, A_scale_sh, B_scale_sh,\n        dtype=dtypes.bf16, bpreshuffle=True,\n    )\n"
}
